zone: The 1928 Strip · the town's library and the archive of the field

front.k: Expanse Gate and the 1928 Strip · Stage Three
front.p: A Mission Revival library in the way the old border towns built their civic buildings: lime stucco on a cantera stone plinth, red barrel tile, a front arcade of eight arches and the doorway, a curvilinear parapet over the door and a clock tower with a tiled dome. Inside are the reading room and, behind a vault door, the 1928 Archive.

tower.p: A square tower with a bell in the belfry, a tiled dome and a weathervane in the shape of a biplane. The clock keeps desert time, and nobody minds if it runs a little slow.

fountain.p: Talavera tile in cobalt, ochre and terracotta round a small stone bowl. A quiet trickle and a cool rim to sit on before you go in.

patio.p: A wall fountain of talavera tile on the archive wing, benches in its shade and a desert willow. A good place to read outside in the morning.

arcade.p: Eight round arches on square piers, a saltillo floor and a timber ceiling: the shady walk along the front, lit by iron lanterns after dark.

tables.p: Long oak tables with green-shaded banker's lamps. Borrow a book from the librarian at the desk, then sit at any table to read it.

stacks.p: Oak bookcases on two levels: the ground floor holds the lending shelves, the gallery above holds reference, atlases and the high desert collection. Rolling ladders run on brass rails.

gallery.p: Up the tiled stair: the gallery runs the length of the room under the clerestory windows, with the reference shelves and the rolling ladders.

ladder.p: Oak and brass on a rail, so the top shelves are never out of reach. Press E again to roll it along.

fire.p: A cantera stone fireplace with a carved mantel and two leather armchairs facing the fire. Sit and stay a while.

catalog.p: Sixty oak drawers of cards: a title, an author and a shelf mark on each, filed by hand. The librarian finds anything in it faster than you can ask.

beams.p: King-post trusses of dark timber, the tie beams painted in the Spanish Colonial way: oxide red, ochre, indigo and cream.

vault.p: The archive sits behind a round steel vault door, kept open in reading hours. Inside: the story of the field, the town on the line and the smelter that built it.

mural.p: The town opened its airfield on the valley floor, a stone's throw from the line. A packed-earth field, a hangar and a windsock: where the runway began. The painting is an artist's impression of opening day, and the case below holds a model of a field of that time.

propeller.p: Laminated hardwood, shaped by hand and sheathed in brass at the tips. Propellers like this one pulled the biplanes and trainers of the 1920s: open cockpits, wood, wire and fabric, an engine up front.

map.p: Two towns on one valley floor with the line between them: this one, laid out on the open flats of the wide valley, and its neighbour across the line. The smelter, the railroad and the field beyond the town. A hand-drawn map of the valley, redrawn for the archive.

photos.p: A biplane at its hangar on a packed-earth field, the smelter stacks over the town, a main street on the line with the depot at its end, and a crowd round a biplane on an opening day. Prints made in the style of the period.

smelter.k: The 1928 Archive · copper and the border town
smelter.p: For decades copper from the mines up the road was smelted here, and the young town grew fast round the stacks. The green malachite and blue azurite in the case are copper ores; the miner's lamp and the assay balance come from the same working world.

model.k: The 1928 Archive · in the glass case
model.p: A scale model of a 1928-style open-cockpit trainer, like the biplane over the Sunfield Terminal and the one in the 1928 Airfield Museum beside the Tower.

timeline.p: The 1900s: the town is laid out beside the border, and the smelter years begin. Rails and ranches tie the valley to the country. The 1920s: barnstormers land on the valley floor. Then the airfield opens: packed earth, a hangar and a windsock. Today the same field flies on as Sunfield.

flatfiles.p: Flat files of old map sheets, field plans and rolled maps, each drawer labelled by hand. Ask at the desk and the librarian will bring one out.

librarian.name: Graciela Ortiz
greet: The archive is through the vault door, at the far end.

talk.t: Welcome to the Expanse Library. The reading room is open to everyone, and the 1928 Archive is through the vault door at the far end. Would you like to borrow a book?
Today's picks from the returns cart. Take one, then find a seat at any reading table.

The archive keeps the story of the field: opening day, a wooden propeller, the old map of the two towns on the line, photographs of the era and the smelter years. Read every case and you will know this valley better than most.
Pick a book here, carry it to any reading table and sit down to read. Bring it back whenever you are done, and take another.

librarian.borrowed: {t} is yours to read. Find a seat at any reading table and sit down to open it.
librarian.returned: Thank you. {t} goes back on the cart. Another?
librarian.out: You already have {t}. Read it at a table, or return it and take another.

p: The first flyers came down on the valley floor when it was still open range, and the cattle stood and watched them. Before long there was a field: packed earth, a hangar and a windsock, and a town that came out in its Sunday clothes to see the wheels touch down.
On a clear morning you could see the whole valley from a thousand feet: the grid of the town, the stacks of the smelter, the line, and the next town over beyond it.
Before dawn the stacks were already smoking. The shift whistle carried across both towns, and the ore trains came down from the mountains night and day.
People came from everywhere for the work, and stayed for the town that grew up round it.
On a clear October night the Milky Way rises over the far ridge like smoke from a long fire. Find the Summer Triangle low in the west, then follow the river of stars south to Sagittarius.
Dry air at four thousand feet is a gift to anyone with a pair of eyes and a little patience.

books.t: A Field Guide to the High Desert
p: Creosote, mesquite and the tall flowering stalks of agave: the high desert keeps its water close. After a summer storm the creosote smells like rain for days.
Look for the palo verde by its green bark. It makes its food in the trunk when the leaves are gone.
Dear Elena, the new field opened today and half the town across the line came over to see it. Your brother swears he will fly before he is twenty. I told him to finish his homework first.
Write soon. The swallows are back under the depot roof.

A little biplane lived in a wooden hangar at the edge of a very big desert. Every morning the windsock told her which way the wind blew, and every morning she said: today I will fly over the mountains.
And one bright morning, she did.

read: I have read this one three times.
stacks: Third shelf from the top, I am sure of it.
The atlases are up in the gallery.
Someone always borrows the one I want.
archive: That propeller is taller than I am.
You can find the field on the map.
Look at the stacks in that photograph.
fire: Nothing like a fire and a book.
fore: The tower clock is right, for once.
I always sit by the fountain before I go in.
Listen, you can hear the bell.
